@emilio do you have any thoughts on this?
@domenic advice for how to get this to build would be greatly appreciated

> This isn't the right structure. It's not a new attribute; it's a new value for an existing attribute.

Ok, I tried putting it within the attr-hidden section.

> Importantly, you need to modify the definition of the attribute from being a boolean attribute to an enumerated attribute, as discussed in #6040.

I removed the sentence that says its a boolean attribute, and I didn't notice any other text that seemed contradictory to having 3 states. How does it look?

> Also, please make sure the spec builds correctly before sending the PR for review.

My bad, I was having trouble with the definitions. It now builds locally on my machine, but on github it's saying that I'm doing something wrong with nested `<ol>` tags, but I don't really understand because I already made a very similar section for auto-expanding details: https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/interactive-elements.html#ancestor-details-revealing-algorithm

Because "hidden" attribute at present is boolean attribute, "hidden" attribute can have a value of empty or "hidden".
Does this PR mean that the "hidden" attribute is no longer boolean attribute?
Does this PR mean that the "hidden" attribute can have a value of empty, "hidden" or "until-found"?

Yes, this is no longer a boolean attribute. It will become an enumerated attribute with three states, per https://github.com/whatwg/html/issues/6040#issuecomment-786861871. ("hidden" is not a valid value, though the empty string is.)

@domenic 

> Yes, this is no longer a boolean attribute. It will become an enumerated attribute with three states, per [#6040 (comment)](https://github.com/whatwg/html/issues/6040#issuecomment-786861871). ("hidden" is not a valid value, though the empty string is.)

That would make currently conforming documents using `hidden="hidden"` invalid. That seems unnecessary, `hidden` can continue to be an allowed value, no?

edit: from the spec

> If the attribute is present, its value must either be the empty string or a value that is an ASCII case-insensitive match for the attribute's canonical name, with no leading or trailing whitespace.

https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/common-microsyntaxes.html#boolean-attributes

> That would make currently conforming documents using hidden="hidden" invalid. That seems unnecessary, hidden can continue to be an allowed value, no?

My goal is to keep *all* of the same behavior with regards to the hidden attribute and `element.hidden`, except when you assign `'until-found'` into it.

> > That would make currently conforming documents using hidden="hidden" invalid. That seems unnecessary, hidden can continue to be an allowed value, no?
> 
> My goal is to keep _all_ of the same behavior with regards to the hidden attribute and `element.hidden`, except when you assign `'until-found'` into it.

Then the value "hidden" should be a valid keyword, in addition to the empty string, both mapping to the *hidden* state.

(See https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/interaction.html#attr-autocapitalize for an example of an enumerated attribute with multiple values mapping to the same state.)

Maybe the prose could be something like this:

> The `hidden` content attribute is an enumerated attribute which (does something). The keywords for this attribute and their state mappings are as follows:
>
> Keyword | State
> ---|----
> The empty string | hidden
> `hidden` | (same cell as above)
> `until-found` | hidden-until-found
>
> The invalid value default is the hidden state. The missing value default is the not-hidden state.
Thank you for the edits @zcorpan!
@emilio you can use author CSS to override the `display: none` in legacy UAs.

> @emilio you can use author CSS to override the `display: none` in legacy UAs.

Right, my point is that it's very easy for the page to forget that, but maybe it's not such a huge issue, unclear...

> So, not necessarily opposed to this, but I'm a bit concerned about backwards compat here. If you use hidden=until-found, that means that UAs that don't yet support this value use display: none. It seems easy for pages to reveal stuff using content-visibility but not display, in which case elements would remain hidden forever... > > Not sure I have a great solution for that though. The explainer mentions something about backwards compat, but how do we plan to address this kind of issue? Yeah, I agree the current state isn't perfect since as I explain in the non-normative note of this PR there may still be box decorations rendered with content-visibility:hidden. I tried out two different mitigations to make hidden=until-found appear more like hidden in these cases: 1. Add the following styles to html.css: ```css [hidden=until-found] { visibility: hidden; } [hidden=until-found] > * { visibility: visible; } ``` I tried it out here: https://chromium-review.googlesource.com/c/chromium/src/+/3322021 This would make the hidden=until-found div not take up space, but there are two problems: - Adding these styles [hits a DCHECK in the style engine](https://chromium-review.googlesource.com/c/chromium/src/+/3322021/1/third_party/blink/renderer/core/html/resources/html.css#1451) which says that we shouldn't include attribute selectors in html.css (which is why we put attribute selectors in the "presentational styles") - This could sort of clash with styles in the page with code like this: ```html
can find content?
``` 2. Don't paint the box decorations. I tried this out here: https://chromium-review.googlesource.com/c/chromium/src/+/3359216 This seems like an improvement, but the box decorations still take up layout space, which honestly seems even worse to me. Imagine you have a black border around the hidden=until-found div, and instead of the developer noticing that its still there when the div is hidden=until-found and removing it, we would just be adding secret extra uncolored space that they might not notice, and then their site would diverge on browsers that do and don't implement hidden=until-found because there is extra space around it... It would be nice if we could figure out some way to not layout the box decorations at all, but I'm not sure where to do this and I'm even less sure of how to spec it. Since hidden=until-found is a new feature, I'm hoping that developers will notice when their hidden=until-found elements have box decorations and remove them when hidden=until-found is present so that it renders the same across browsers that do and don't implement this. > It seems easy for pages to reveal stuff using content-visibility but not display, in which case elements would remain hidden forever... Now that I read this again, are you just concerned with the backwards compat of the actual revealing functionality, not just the box decorations while hidden...?

> Now that I read this again, are you just concerned with the backwards compat of the actual revealing functionality, not just the box decorations while hidden...?

Yeah, that's right. The box decorations when hidden is a sorta-expected side-effect of `content-visibility: hidden`, right?

> So, not necessarily opposed to this, but I'm a bit concerned about backwards compat here. If you use hidden=until-found, that means that UAs that don't yet support this value use display: none. It seems easy for pages to reveal stuff using content-visibility but not display, in which case elements would remain hidden forever...

> Yeah, that's right. The box decorations when hidden is a sorta-expected side-effect of content-visibility: hidden, right?

So it sounds like the potential slight differences in rendering is OK, but having an element that "would remain hidden forever" is the concern? If a page makes a hidden=until-found element which can *only* be revealed by find-in-page, ScrollToTextFragment, or fragment navigation in supported browsers, then I think that's the page's problem. I believe that any time this feature is used, the page should provide an alternative way to expand the content like a button, just like the details element has.

> So it sounds like the potential slight differences in rendering is OK, but having an element that "would remain hidden forever" is the concern? If a page makes a hidden=until-found element which can _only_ be revealed by find-in-page, ScrollToTextFragment, or fragment navigation in supported browsers, then I think that's the page's problem. I believe that any time this feature is used, the page should provide an alternative way to expand the content like a button, just like the details element has.

Yeah, my concern was more about the page doing something like revealing just setting `content-visibility: visible` or `auto` (think via a class toggle or the style attribute or so), in which case UAs that don't implement _either_ content-visibility or `hidden=until-found` will never be able to show the content (for different reasons). Not sure whether there's a whole lot we can do, though it'd be nice to have better fallback here.

> Yeah, my concern was more about the page doing something like revealing just setting content-visibility: visible or auto (think via a class toggle or the style attribute or so), in which case UAs that don't implement either content-visibility or hidden=until-found will never be able to show the content (for different reasons). Not sure whether there's a whole lot we can do, though it'd be nice to have better fallback here.

Thanks for elaborating! I still don't fully understand though... could you write out a more concrete example?

If I understand correctly, the scenario is:

A website uses `hidden=until-found`, and provides a button for users to reveal the content. Instead of removing the `hidden` attribute (which would work OK), the author changed the styling with `content-visibility: visible`. The author only tested in browsers that support `content-visibility` and sees that it works.

In browsers that don't support `content-visibility` (and also don't support `hidden=until-found`), the content is always hidden with `display: none`.

Is that correct @emilio?

We could clarify with an example or something in the spec that the appropriate way to make an element no longer be hidden is by removing the `hidden` attribute.

Thanks for elaborating @zcorpan 

> We could clarify with an example or something in the spec that the appropriate way to make an element no longer be hidden is by removing the hidden attribute.

Yeah I think a note would be best, I'm really not sure of a way around this unless we want to put !important on the rule or something, which feels wrong...
Yeah, plus `!important` isn't usually a thing in presentation attributes. But yeah, that was the scenario I was describing, thanks zcorpan.

Ok, I believe that I've addressed all the comments.
@domenic @zcorpan I'll merge this when both of you have approved since you're both in the "changes requested" state.

> You need to add the onbeforematch content and IDL attributes too. If you Ctrl+F for onclose in the spec you should find all the locations:

Ok, `onbeforematch` now has parity with `onclose`. Thanks!

> interface mixin GlobalEventHandlers mixin

Wait, are you sure I should add this to GlobalEventHandlers? Why would it be helpful to add a beforematch event handler to `window` or `document`?

> Wait, are you sure I should add this to GlobalEventHandlers? Why would it be helpful to add a beforematch event handler to `window` or `document`?

It's a bit strange, but basically for consistency and simplicity.

For events that bubble, using `document.oninput = ...` can be useful for event delegation, so we put events like `input` into `GlobalEventHandlers`. And then we decided it's not worthwhile to figure out, for each global event, whether it will ever bubble or not, or whether it will apply to windows or not, and carefully place it in `HTMLElement` or `DocumentAndElementEventHandlers` or `GlobalEventHandlers`. We just place everything into `GlobalEventHandlers` and don't worry about it.

While implementing the IDL changes in chromium, I made a webui (chrome:// pages) test fail because it was doing `element.hidden = 0`. If webui does this, then I think its likely that other websites do too, so I think we should add `unrestricted double` to the IDL to detect numbers and handle this appropriately. I just pushed a commit to do this. @domenic @zcorpan what do you think?

> While implementing the IDL changes in chromium, I made a webui (chrome:// pages) test fail because it was doing `element.hidden = 0`. If webui does this, then I think its likely that other websites do too, so I think we should add `unrestricted double` to the IDL to detect numbers and handle this appropriately.

I would be surprised if undefined/null weren't also common, e.g. `elem.hidden = anyExpressionUsedForItsTruthiness`. Unlike string and number, Boolean coercion isn't "stigmatized" in most JS idioms the way other coercion often is. But this union is already pretty weird (is there precedent for it?)

> I would be surprised if undefined/null weren't also common, e.g. elem.hidden = anyExpressionUsedForItsTruthiness

undefined and null are also specially handled to be backwards compatible in this change because I added a `?` in the IDL. (Thanks for suggesting this @zcorpan!)

> But this union is already pretty weird 

I agree it's weird. Ideally, `boolean or DOMString` would convert all non-string types to booleans instead of strings, but at least in chromium it chooses strings, so we need this special handling.

> (is there precedent for it?)

No, I'm not sure there are other IDLs that have run into this problem.

Thanks, missed that it was already nullable. And including a numeric type is (almost) like adjusting the order of [steps 14 and 17](https://webidl.spec.whatwg.org/#es-union) of union conversion - makes sense.

> [Tests](https://github.com/web-platform-tests/wpt) are written and can be reviewed and commented upon at:

We should be sure there are tests for the UA stylesheet. https://github.com/web-platform-tests/wpt/issues/5625 discusses the general issue but we could instead do targeted tests. Basically:

- Test that `hidden=""` and `hidden=asdf` on a `div` give `display: none` and leave `content-visibility` at its default value.
- Test that `hidden=until-found` and `hidden=UNTIL-foUNd` on a `div` give `content-visibility: hidden` and leave `display` at its default value.
- Test that `hidden=""` and `hidden=asdf` and `hidden=until-found` give `display: inline; width: 0; height: 0;` on an `embed` and leave `content-visibility` at its default value.
- Test that `hidden=""` and `hidden=asdf` and `hidden=until-found` give the appropriate values for all special table elements: https://whatpr.org/html/7475/rendering.html#tables-2 and don't touch `content-visibility`.

> We should be sure there are tests for the UA stylesheet

I started a test here: https://chromium-review.googlesource.com/c/chromium/src/+/3529819

Unfortunately, I think I found some issues with hidden attributes on embeds and tables.

For embeds, it looks like the `display:inline` works as it says in the spec, but the `width:0px` and `height:0px` [only apply if hidden is "yes" or "true"](https://source.chromium.org/chromium/chromium/src/+/main:third_party/blink/renderer/core/html/html_embed_element.cc;l=82-83;drc=efb59b0cefb13faf55cce3066809f11f99ab9ab8), and only in webkit and chromium: https://jsfiddle.net/jarhar/a17exs2g/

For tables, I tried the first element in the user agent stylesheet from the spec, the colgroup element. I found that instead of applying `display:table-column-group` when hidden like the spec says, it does `display:none` in all browsers: https://jsfiddle.net/jarhar/74Lqx1uf/
Maybe the `[hidden]` should be removed from these table elements in the spec?

`embed[hidden]` style was specced in https://github.com/whatwg/html/commit/b0e1a3e73575a1966db09f7d42112d5fc0f76eb0 to fix https://www.w3.org/Bugs/Public/show_bug.cgi?id=15133 (browsers impl predated the spec)

`colgroup[hidden]` style was specced in https://github.com/whatwg/html/commit/27f2a83d5feb757a031957045eeb51b7dbe1623a - I can't find any relevant discussion for this change.

Are you aware that normalize.css has declarations for [hidden] already:
https://github.com/necolas/normalize.css/blob/fc091cce1534909334c1911709a39c22d406977b/normalize.css#L347-L349

I have seen similar declarations in many projects and I wonder if this will not result in an unconscious opt-out?

> I have seen similar declarations in many projects and I wonder if this will not result in an unconscious opt-out?

Yes, that will result in an opt-out. Auto-expanding details has a similar issue where sites make `details:not([open]) > *` display:none as well, but that ended up actually being a useful way to opt-out for websites that didn't want the auto-expanding behavior. For this feature, hopefully developers would notice that hidden=until-found isn't working in this case, but I'm not sure how I would detect this scenario and add a console message for it or otherwise help developers with this. Do you have any suggestions?

Maybe you can identify the most common sources (like normalize.css) and file issues suggesting to replace with
```
[hidden=""], [hidden="hidden"] { display: none }
```
This would not hide elements with `hidden=until-found` in really old browsers that don't support the `hidden` attribute, but, maybe that's not an issue? Maybe the suggestion should be to remove the rule altogether, instead.

> Then again, I just realized that now that we made "until-found" case insensitive, this selector wouldn't catch hidden=UNTIL-FOUND... is there a selector I can make that would capture all cases? Should we change this feature to be only lowercase "until-found" to address this?

Could "hidden" be safely added to the [list of HTML attributes whose values CSS selectors must match case-insensitively](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/#case-sensitivity-of-selectors)? It _seems_ like this list is meant for stuff like this, though I’m only inferring that and don’t know that for sure.

(It’s possible that web content could exist that’s relying on its sensitivity today, but this seems pretty unlikely given it was boolean before + the same could be said about other aspects of this change anyway.)
We're already using `[hidden=until-found i]` in the style sheet. The `i` makes it case-insensitive.

> Could "hidden" be safely added to the [list of HTML attributes whose values CSS selectors must match case-insensitively](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/#case-sensitivity-of-selectors)?

No, that list is not intended to have full coverage of attributes that are case-insensitive in HTML, it's intended to be web compatible. So new case-insensitive attributes should not be added. Also, `hidden` was already case-insensitive before this change, since it was a boolean attribute (`hidden="HIDDEN"` is valid).

>  We're already using [hidden=until-found i] in the style sheet. The i makes it case-insensitive.

> As for case-insensitive value, the i flag can be used in author CSS as well

I didn't know about this, thanks!

> but in legacy browsers that don't support it the whole ruleset will be dropped. Since the rule is intended for old browsers (that don't support the hidden attribute), this is relevant

I see... it doesn't seem like there is a perfect option to update normalize.css with.

> No, that list is not intended to have full coverage of attributes that are case-insensitive in HTML, it's intended to be web compatible. So new case-insensitive attributes should not be added. Also, hidden was already case-insensitive before this change, since it was a boolean attribute (hidden="HIDDEN" is valid)

Thanks for the info! It sounds like this PR doesn't need any updates. @domenic can we merge this?
We're waiting on tests for the UA stylesheet, per https://github.com/whatwg/html/pull/7475#issuecomment-1069313217, before we can merge.
Tests for the UA stylesheet have been merged here: https://github.com/web-platform-tests/wpt/pull/33221
Awesome! I've merged the spec. Please file Gecko and WebKit bugs, and edit the original post with links to them.

> I see... it doesn't seem like there is a perfect option to update normalize.css with.

Yeah. I think my proposal in https://github.com/whatwg/html/pull/7475#issuecomment-1071690599 strikes the right balance, as almost all cases will either use minimized syntax (`<div hidden>`)  or the long form and lowercase (`<div hidden="hidden">`).
